utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by asking you about some of the duties and tasks that you had described earlier to us. Now, you had explained that you did not report to Momir Nikolic; you reported to -- generally, you reported to the brigade commander. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You did, on occasion, work with Momir Nikolic, you explained, and one of those occasions is when you were looking into searching for weapons, as you explained, in some of the humanitarian convoys going into the Srebrenica enclave. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were checking the deliveries of humanitarian aid to the effect of checking whether there were any armaments there as well, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, do you remember approximately how many times you were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with precision; 30 times, 20 times, or something of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Over what time frame would those 20 or 30 times have been?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the time frame would be about a year, perhaps a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And a year beginning and ending when? Ending -- I mean, would that be July 1994 to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall with precision. It was from the beginning they starting delivering humanitarian aid, and when that started exactly I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, how would this process work? Would you search these convoys for weapons yourself or would you have assistance from someone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- I didn't do the searches myself personally. It was the patrol of the military police that had been assigned for that day on the part of the commander of the police or the chief, Momir Nikolic. I was only the person who dealt with the paper so that the whole procedure would be signed to the effect that an inspection had been made, everything was all right. And to inventory, or rather, take a list of the ID cards of the humanitarian personnel that was transporting the humanitarian relief supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these documents, including this inventory, in a normal course of your work you would forward that to the brigade commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, that was not the customary procedure. If it happened that they were indeed transporting something which was not on the list, if hidden weapons were found or ammunition among the goods being transported, then in such cases the commander had to be so informed through the security organ. However, there wasn't a single such incident. We never found anything which was out of the ordinary, which was irregular, except for some goods which were in a way being transported on these vehicles without having been recorded, accounted for. But these were minor problems, of course, which could be and were resolved in a tolerant fashion in situ, right there. So if I am not too extensive, such objects could not have been driven anywhere in the formal humanitarian assistance but would be returned. They could not enter Srebrenica. In other words, they would be temporarily seized, and when they - I mean the convoy - returned, the officials would then take over those goods and return them; they would be restituted to them. The alternative was, according to the suggestion of the commander, that if Momir Nikolic with his men could not carry this out, that either he or the leader of the -- the commander of the military police should assign a patrol -- not a patrol, rather, a group of soldiers who would search the vehicles, and that I was to get involved in this by controlling the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say that this group of soldiers would search the vehicles and you would get involved at the suggestion of the commander, you're talking about your commander, the brigade commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, the commander of the brigade who was the commander of the brigade then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And your immediate supervisor, as you had previously explained, in your normal course of duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not officially. This was rather an oral suggestion by the commander. "If he should not be there, you are there and you do the task. I know that you will do it properly." It was not officially prescribed that this or that person should be doing this or that task. I did a hundred tasks which were not written anywhere as my particular assignment. These were minor things and the commander entrusted them to me because he had confidence in me that I would discharge them diligently, properly, and that is why I had to do it. Of course, I accepted it; one does not refuse one's commander, even if it is a simple letter. If I could draw it up better than he could, for instance, or similar. It wasn't a rigid procedure, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these requests, oral or otherwise, made to you by your commander, this is something that continued when Mr. Blagojevic became the brigade commander, right, it didn't change?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I didn't do any checking, if that is what you are asking. I no longer did any checking. I did it for a while, and after that, a checking point was established at the Zuti Most, the yellow bridge, with persons particularly assigned with controlling deliveries of humanitarian aid to Srebrenica. If that is what you are referring to. As for the other things, these are minor, petty matters. It was only normal, and I believe the commander Blagojevic really had confidence in me that I would, indeed, discharge these minor matters efficiently, and it was not something that was strictly official, according to my regulations of sphere of activity. After all, no one had precisely defined my job description at all. This was a practice which was inaugurated at the beginning of the war, and it remained as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, where would you maintain these documents, the inventories of material coming in or records about material that hadn't been properly set out in the paperwork for the trucks coming in? These kinds of documents, where would you maintain them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the search, the inspection, whosoever was doing the inspection, a person like myself but a person who was doing that part of the job would be given a copy of the transportation lists specifying the products, the goods, that were being transported, that were being driven away. And I kept the papers in my office. If this was done by Momir Nikolic, he would keep it, and what he did with it, I don't know. But there were no special reasons for this documentation to be kept as some kind of special records. No one required that of us, and in view of the fact that this inspection was carried out without any problems whatsoever and that these people from international organisations were delivering humanitarian assistance to Srebrenica behaved very correctly, indeed transporting the goods which were on the lists. We never found any forbidden goods, or in other words, ammunition of weapons, at least not whilst I was discharging that particular duty. So having this clean situation, nothing could be disputed or disputable, so we had no particular reason to safeguard or deposit anywhere this information or keep it, because we were not maintaining any statistical -- statistics on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celanovic, I would like to move to another one of your -- another one of the functions you've explained to us. You told us you collected statements and information regarding crimes committed against Serbian people. Now, you collected that information from both victims and also, as you explained to us, from witnesses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Witnesses and -- not victims, the victims were dead. I interviewed the survivors, that is, the population of a village that had been attacked, had been destroyed, those who had survived and whose family members had been killed in such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you conducted -- you gathered this information -- of course even though there had been no arrests? No one had been arrested and brought in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whom you mean specifically. No one could be arrested at that time just for being a witness. I actually do not understand your question. Please, could you formulate this more specifically. Who was to have been arrested and why? I didn't exactly get it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's okay. I'll -- let me restate that. You conducted this work even though there had been no suspects brought before you. No one had been arrested by the military police and brought before you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you explained that, regarding the Muslims who were being held in detention in Bratunac on and about the 13th of July, that you heard only a few days later that they had all been killed. Now, you never took any statements in connection with trying to uncover what happened to them, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You never questioned anyone about that as part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not, because I had no investigative powers. I already explained that only once they brought someone to me according to the orders of somebody else was I able to take a statement. And I personally at no time had in the powers to undertake any investigation, neither under the law nor according to orders. This was the duty of military and civilian judicial organs of the prosecutorial organs and the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You never suggested any criminal investigations -- you never suggested that criminal investigations be undertaken? You never suggested that to your commander or anyone else, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You didn't even suggest that there be any disciplinary measures taken in this regard, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't up to me to make such proposals. Mine was to work as instructed. I was not empowered to give any suggestions to the commander until he asked me to. And this problem actually overcame, exceeded, the bounds of the brigade, of the commander, of a simple ordinary lawyer, desk officer. It was quite clear that this was the work of the state of the government of the judiciary of the police and of The Hague Tribunal, after all, which had already existed at the time. So I believe that not even the commander had the kind of powers required, if he didn't have the right information. Actually, he had no powers to instruct me and to undertake any investigation. And had he instructed me to undertake any investigation out of bounds of my powers or in contravention to some legal provisions according to which I can act, I would have refused, because it is not my competence to do so. As a jurist, I knew full well at that time as well who was in charge of what and who had what competences. Let me not repeat; I do not wish to belabour the point, and tire both you and the Trial Chamber, these were the civilian and military judicial organs which were bound under the law to undertake, after such a horrendous crime, to do their very best in order to detect the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, are you telling us -- let me ask you this: If a Muslim were killed in Bratunac on the night of 13th of July, would it not be within the authority of the brigade commander to request or order some investigation, some inquiry?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned to us yesterday that the fact that all these people, thousands of people, had been killed was known generally. Soldiers were talking about it and civilians were talking about it. Just so we're clear, you never received any instructions or orders from Colonel Blagojevic to undertake any inquiries or any other information collection in this regard. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes, I never received any such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess he also knew that other organs were in charge of that. I believe that he knew that. He knew what my powers were, that I was not authorised to undertake any investigations in the sense of a conventional police inspector or investigating magistrate or prosecutor, which are the organs that are officially entitled to undertake such investigations. I perhaps am extensive in explaining. But if you allow me, I have already said before what the procedure was to be observed when a murder happened. In all fairness, this was in cases when a soldier of the Bratunac Brigade killed another soldier or civilian. Then where there was some preliminary criminal actions that we had to undertake in the way which I have already described. This was a totally different situation all together. And I don't know. These moments you say it was the 13th or any other date around that time. I don't know how much people knew as to whether any murders had been committed or not. I had not received any orders to the effect that I was to undertake any inquiries or investigations. And I myself did not have the authority to do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I think you've answered my question and some others as well. If I could just now continue on to talk about some of your other duties. I just want to make sure we got this right. In connection with -- and you've explained to us that -- you've explained this to us before, in the case of a disciplinary breach you would take statements, prepare other documents, and you would report it to your commander, the brigade commander. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if requested you would provide advice on what sort of actions or steps the brigade commander could take in regards to such a disciplinary breach. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the same way in the case of a potential criminal act you would take statements and provide documents, and you would provide that to your brigade commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If these persons -- if persons were brought to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who had committed some -- any offence or misdemeanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've explained that. Now, you also explained to us that in the case of detainees, whether soldiers or civilians, you would also take statements from them and you would provide it to the commander and to the chief of the security organ. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also explained that it would be the brigade commander who would make sure that prisoners of war were sent to a detention facility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. But if you allow me just a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Certainly, a brief correction if necessary.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be brief. It was not always the commander of the brigade. At times it was -- if you observe the genesis of the brigade's formation, first it was the commander of the garrison, the commander of the battalion, and then a commander of the brigade. So it was not always the commander of the brigade, but it was always the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We understand that. And yet you told us despite all these regular functions, when you took these notes from these -- from these five persons who were brought to you on the 13th of July and the sixth person, Mr. Resid Sinanovic, on this one occasion you did not provide this information to your brigade commander. And just tell me if that's correct. If that's correct, then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these were not detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, you've told us they were sent to detention at the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something else, yes. That is correct. That was the reception or collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: They were brought to you by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were brought there for another reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: They could not have walked away, could they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a document, Mr. Celanovic. It's -- the document is Prosecution Exhibit 445. If you could just take a minute to read that document, and I'll just bring your attention to a couple of specific points in it. Have you had a chance to look at it, Mr. Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You see at the top it's -- at the top it says: "Drina Corps command intelligence section." And it's dated 12 July 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's marked right afterwards. It's marked: "Very urgent." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very urgent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the second page at the bottom you see that it has the signature block of General Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Top first page, you see the addressees. Do you see where it includes the chiefs of intelligence organs. And it includes the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, under the addressees list - and you see that there are several other brigades listed there - there's a line that says: "This is the statement by prisoner of war Izudin Bektic." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, the first paragraph indicates that this is a man who was taken prisoner about 1800 hours on the 12th of July near Kajici?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You know where Kajici is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The next paragraph you see a name that we've seen in some of your notes, Zulfo, Zulfo Tursunovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The next line reads -- and I'll go slowly, I apologise to the interpreters; we probably didn't provide this either. "He assessed that a group of about 500 armed Muslims, including children and unmarried women fit for military service, set off under Zulfo's commander on 11 July this year." My apologies to the interpreters, if that was okay. This Zulfo, of course, appears in some of the notes you took from these six persons who were brought to you on the 13th of July. Now, Mr. Celanovic, my question for you is simple here: This is an urgent report sent to a number of brigades about -- that discusses the location of Zulfo and some of his men taken from a prisoner. I mean, that would be a fair characterisation of what this document is, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, this is urgent -- this is an urgent report and the subject matter here is important because lives depend on it, I mean, lives of Serbian soldiers in that area depended on intelligence and information about where the Muslims were. That's obvious, isn't it, Mr. Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you disagree with me, that lives of the Serbian soldiers did not depend on timely intelligence about the location of Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the Serbian soldiers were right at that moment, so I can see neither yes or no. I'm afraid I won't be saying the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, I'm not asking you where the Serbian soldiers were. I'm asking you simply as a general matter, isn't it true that the safety of Serbian soldiers --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let the answer be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So you would agree with me, then. You were getting the same kind of information, where Zulfo might have been heading, you were getting that from these people brought to you on the 13th of July, and even when the lives of Serbian soldiers were at stake, it never occurred to you to forward that to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious from this letter who did this, who was involved in this. It's the security organs; and I was not one of them. I did not have instructions to ask where the troops were. I have been repeating this time and again. I was just supposed to ask where Naser's unit commanders were, including Zulfo. Because we had their names in our records as suspects. Namely, they were suspected of having torched Serb villages and killed civilians, that is to say, having committed war crimes. If I asked about Zulfo, one person would say he didn't know where he was; another person would say he went through the hills. So even without my questions, these people spontaneously spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, if I could -- we've discussed already this issue about the spontaneous statements of these people. My question to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I believe he's answered the question. If the gentleman would please listen to the answer. Yesterday I didn't object. There were several occasions where he asked the same question over and over again; he's received his answer, that he wasn't a member of the security and intelligence, that's why he didn't have to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the message is very clear in the transcript. And I hope that both the Prosecutor and the witness could ask or answer their questions as concise as possible, because we have spent so much time. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I will just ask you one question here, Mr. Celanovic. Even if you had not been tasked, if you learned of a large armed Muslim group moving through the area where you knew Bratunac Brigade soldiers or other soldiers of the Republika Srpska were, are you telling us that you would not give that information to anyone simply because you had not been asked to do -- to collect that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I address the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some questions that I simply cannot give mere yes or no answers to. I don't want a single answer of mine not to reflect the truth. I don't want it to look that way, that I'm not telling the truth. I do apologise to the Prosecutor, but what can you say to confused questions? You can only give a confused answer. As for these military groups in the field, there were intelligence organs there and our units were there. I was the last person to find out what was going on. There was not a single reason why I would know spontaneously, or rather, that I would receive a statement, a spontaneous statement, from a person and that I would know which troops were where in an enclave or wherever. Had it -- had the situation been different, than perhaps I would have found out some other way. For example, when a worried soldier, a member of the brigade -- I mean, I would share my information with whom I was supposed to share that information. So this was that personal risk that I ran, whether I am going to transmit that information further or not. My assessment at that moment was that it was not necessary. And I hope that I have given an answer to this last question. I am sorry, but some questions simply cannot be answered by a mere yes or no without getting the wrong impression about my testimony. I keep looking at this solemn statement here. I don't want anybody to have the impression at any point in time that I'm not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Shin, I think you made your point already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move on to the last area -- last topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, I'd like to refer you back to this document, this hospital record for Resid Sinanovic that you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just for the record that's -- that was marked D170 -- I'm sorry, D169.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you can just have it in front of you for reference, Mr. Celanovic. I'm not going to specifically direct your attention to it. Now, you've indicated that that record shows that Mr. Sinanovic was indicated for surgical treatment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, he wasn't as -- you've testified he wasn't injured or hurt when you saw him, was he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And during the time -- during these one or two hours that he was with you or with you and Mr. Davidovic, he was not abused in any way, was he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was accorded every attention, and he was treated as fairly as could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, there's a hospital in Bratunac, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medical centre. It's not really a hospital in the traditional sense of the word; it's like a clinic, a health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. A health centre. And there's a hospital in Zvornik, too, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And there's a hospital in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, where is Loznica, the location of this hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loznica is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposite Bijeljina and Zvornik, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have been more precise. It's in another country; it's not in the Republika Srpska. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that on the 13th of July there were Muslim prisoners in the Bratunac health centre?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you knew that they were under the care of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the representatives of UNPROFOR in front of the health centre in the yard when I came there. Now, whether they were supervising them or whether they were under the care of UNPROFOR, as you had put it, I assumed they were, but I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, are you aware that those people in the Bratunac health centre, those Muslim prisoners -- I'm sorry, those Muslim patients, that they survived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they had survived, those who were at the health centre. As a matter of fact, I heard that a baby was born. I heard that as a positive story, and that the baby was delivered although there were no proper hospital conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, do you know where your friend Resid Sinanovic is today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know if he's alive or if he's dead?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You know that he's listed among the missing on the ICRC's missing list, as well as the other five people who were brought to you on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he's on the list, but he has been recorded as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the ICRC, you've explained to us that among your duties the brigade commander had once tasked you with reporting four or five elderly people being brought to the enclave, or reporting them to the International Red Cross. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, if I could quote you directly you say: "The brigade commander tasked me with reporting them" -- I'm sorry. I'll slow down. "The brigade commander tasked me with reporting them to the International Red Cross or the UNHCR." And then you say a little later: "This'them,' 'reporting them' is a reference to four or five elderly people whom we fed and took care of until the moment when I handed them over to these organisations." You remember that, right? You remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm sorry. Perhaps the interpretation I received was not correct at first. Now, that is correct. That is what I said and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, if Colonel Blagojevic had simply asked you to see the International Red Cross about any of the six people brought to you on the 13th of July, or in fact about any of the detainees at the Vuk Karadzic school, they would be alive today, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. We have Beara, we have Mladic, we had Popovic, we had their own star witness, Nikolic, running around trying to kill everybody they could get their hands on. And to suggest now that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to argue with him as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's an improper question and Mr. McCloskey should sit down. He is not conducting the examination and this is not a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this kind of bile at this time, and argument I will stand up to until this case is over and it's outrageous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is outrageous in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, we have said that we hope that one counsel should deal with one particular witness, unless there is procedure matters that have the general interest or impact. I hope both parties could stick to this rule, otherwise there is no order in this courtroom. Mr. Shin, I believe that your question has some problems. It is a sort of speculation question. Maybe you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. May I address the Court? I can answer the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a small correction, though. It is not Commander Blagojevic. At that time Vuksic was the commander. Commander Vuksic ordered me, let's put it that way; let's say it was an order. The way you put the question, let me try to be brief now. That's the way it was. I handed over these persons to the International Red Cross, and I received a signature. These were old and feeble people. Some people didn't even know when they had been born; they couldn't remember the year. Would that suffice for an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please have the other microphone turned on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation, Mr. Celanovic. So I'll just ask you this: What do you think? Do you think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. He's asking him to speculate. I don't need to hear the rest of the question. He's going to be thinking about whether Colonel Blagojevic had ordered him to go to the Red Cross as if disregarding all the other facts in the matter, such as who was there with the Drina Corps having its forward command post at the Bratunac Brigade, with Mladic having his forward command post at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you talk too much. You know, the Prosecution has not asked this question yet, and in some circumstances the speculation questions could be asked if it's related to the subject matter, or if it's the natural result of the development of the events. Yes, Mr. Shin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, in light of all the duties you have explained to us in detail and in light of this latest explanation you've given us about an order provided to you by Commander Vuksic, do you think if Colonel Blagojevic had asked you to list these people brought to you, register them with the ICRC, do you think they would be alive today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, it calls for speculation. It totally disregards all the other facts that are in place. The fact that you have the military police there, the special police, you have Popovic, you have Beara, you have all the other people --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the hypothetical included all those facts, Your Honour, I would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Karnavas, the logic is that some other people were sent to the ICRC at that time and those people, I guess, survived. And those people that were sent to the so-called reception centre were recorded as missing people. So the logic is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the timing is wrong. Vuksic was the commander at the time when the gentleman delivered the old people. Now we're talking about years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have the right to ask this question in your re-direct. You could -- in your question you could correct anything that is not satisfied to your need. You may sit down, please. Witness, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I've already forgotten the question. Could it please be repeated? I listened to this dialogue between Mr. Karnavas and the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, the question is: In light of all the duties that you have described to us in detail and in light of this latest explanation you have given us about an order provided to you by Commander Vuksic regarding bringing some people to the International Red Cross, do you think if Colonel Blagojevic had asked you to register these five or six people brought to you on the 13th of July with the Red Cross, do you think these people would be alive today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Mr. Blagojevic, the commander, known, had these people been there at the time, had the International Red Cross been there, had there been a great many circumstances involved, I don't know, I cannot say what he would have ordered me to do. But it is only natural that -- regardless of whether it would be my official duty or not, if the order did not entail the commission of a crime, I would have carried out any order given to me. But unfortunately these people were not handed over. I wish they had been handed over; that's what I wish now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you wish they had been handed over, because if they would have been handed over they would have survived, they would be alive now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying today. Today I'm saying -- I don't know whether they would have survived had they been handed over. But then, at that time, I believed that everybody would survive. I -- it never crossed my mind to think about what you're asking me today. I believe that all these people would be alive and well and healthy and transferred to Muslim territory. This never crossed my mind that there would be some kind of selection. And to ask for the International Red Cross to come and to take over some of them, I didn't even know where their headquarters were. And it was not my duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, you said: "I wish they had been handed over; that's what I wish now." And you're saying that because if they had been handed over to the International Red Cross they would be alive now, isn't that the truth? Isn't that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. It's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think the Prosecution is entitled to clarify something in the answer of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, I will ask you again. You said: "I wish" --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. As a human being I'm sorry that these people lost their lives and all other people who lost their lives. That's why I'm sorry that they were not handed over by anyone so they could have survived, even if one person had survived, that would have been a good thing. At a human being, I'm sorry that they did not survive. It didn't have to be me, I didn't have to be involved. But as a human being, I'm sorry. This is not directly related to your question. As a human being, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had the United Nations who set up this Tribunal done its job and kept the enclave demilitarised and kept the Muslim fighters from slaughtering the Serb villagers that were living around Srebrenica, do you think it might have been -- there might not have been any need to attack Srebrenica and try to restrict the enclave back in July 6th, 1995? Had the United Nations done its job?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which it had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This question is out of the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It goes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because I don't believe the Prosecution raised this question in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe it's a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When was Mr. Vuksic the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- let me think for a while. That was some time from February 2003 [sic] until I don't know what time. I don't remember dates well. I'm not good with dates. I know that this happened -- he assumed in February because I was with him before that. He harassed me in a way. There was some incident with him, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be 1993 as opposed to 2003?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was -- it is 1993. I was shocked by this last question of the Prosecutor -- moved, in fact, so I have to collect myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When Mr. Vuksic was there at the commander, had the Main Staff set up its forward command post in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the Drina Corps? Had the Drina Corps set up its command post in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think that there was any reason within the regular, normal, activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether General Mladic was around slapping soldiers, giving orders, kicking officers, as we've heard in this courtroom, in the Bratunac area at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that in the area where the 2nd Battalion was, that is the hill of Caus and Likari, soldiers told these stories, that he had kicked some people and called them cowards and told them to go move ahead, and on. And that he also slapped some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that back in 1993, though, when Vuksic was the commander? That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you were told to take those prisoners -- those elderly folks to the unit's yard, did you have Colonel Beara running around Bratunac along with Popovic? Was he around at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't remember whether he moved about at that time. What I can say is how these prisoners - shall I say - these civilians came to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. How they came to be brought before me, if you want me to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to focus your attention on -- because it's back when Mr. Vuksic was the commander. Okay. Was Beara in the Bratunac area conducting activities during that period of time when Vuksic was there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. He probably was there. He would come occasionally to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade for control purposes and for other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he have units of the special police, MUP, over there conducting activities, as we've heard in this testimony? I'm talking about 1993. Were they there swarming around the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this was when Mr. Vuksic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, are you an advocate? Do you have the licence to practice in a courtroom in criminal matters?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not now, that's right. And in fact, you are what is known as a graduated lawyer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This appears to be beyond the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's right within the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We haven't heard the follow-up question. Let us hear the follow-up question and we'll decide whether those questions are within the scope or not. I believe Mr. Karnavas is laying some foundations for that. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're a graduated lawyer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in order to practice in a courtroom as a defence lawyer or as a prosecutor or to be an investigative judge or to be a judge, you have to have special training, do you not, and not just merely a degree from a law school. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to be admitted to the bar, to pass the bar exam, to pass the exam. And then be admitted to the bar. And then I would be issued a licence to work in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at the time back in 1995 and today as well, you were not admitted into the bar, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So not being admitted into the bar, could you have conducted investigations like an investigative judge, or could you have initiated prosecutions like a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained this a number of times, no. No, I could not. I didn't have the statutory powers for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blagojevic know what Beara had instructed you to do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if he didn't know what you were doing, how he would have known to give you any instructions as to those people that you were questioning?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you be more specific. Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Here. If Colonel Blagojevic did not know what you were doing and who you were questioning, how would he know what instructions to give you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not have known. He didn't see me. I would not see him. I hadn't seen him for three or four days prior to the 13th, nor did I see him after that date nor did I get in touch with him in any way after that date. Nor did Beara tell me to inform anyone about what he had ordered me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I have a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since you were not a lawyer at that time, how could Mr. Blagojevic entrust you to be the head of the commission to investigate some acts to stealing the properties of the brigade commander's post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President of the Court, Chamber, I wish to explain. I wish to explain that no one in this court referred to the law on the army as lex specialis. On the basis of which the commander could have -- could entrust a task to a certain individual, he could entrust a person with - and please pay attention to this term - some inquiry actions, not investigating actions, as defined under this law. So in accordance with this, I, as the president of this commission, was entrusted with a task not to undertake and conduct investigations, but to carry out inventories of property, a simple stock-taking operation, and to seal the premises so inspected, so inventoried, and then to give the key -- and to put the key in an envelope, and along with a record of the inventoried property in the flat, to pass it on to the head of the OB, the security and intelligence organ. So this was the same job, in other words, as that which is executed by members of the ministry for displaced persons and refugees in the restitution of property to returnees exercise. These are actions which do not require either a jurisprudence degree --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your last sentence because the interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So these are tasks which do not require a jurisprudence degree. So any vocational background is enough for that. You could be a construction technician, a civil engineering secondary education will suffice for this, for the inventorying and sealing of certain premises. Even the Administrative Procedure Act foresees that this should be done by persons even in state organs of this profile. I gave you an example, for instance, in the case of the workers in the ministry for refugees and displaced persons and refugees, who are not lawyers, not jurists, but have made hundreds of thousands of minutes and records of this type. As members of the commission, I hope that I have managed to reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions out of my question? Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. D167, which is from the command of the Bratunac Brigade. D168, this is a crime investigation report from Mr. Celanovic. D169, which is the letter from -- letter to Mr. Londrovic regarding the medical records. D170, which is the decree on temporary usage of houses to show that those who had left could retain ownership. And then D172, the order that established the commission regarding the apartment concerning the last question by you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents are admitted into the evidence. On the part of the Prosecution, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's a document marked P859. It is the witness statement of Mr. Celanovic taken by the Republika Srpska MUP in Bratunac on the 28th of August, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Keeping with the rules, if we're going to stick by the rules, as Mr. McCloskey keeps reminding us, we break it once, we break it a thousand, I believe that was his quote of the day, of that day, statements don't come in. Unless there's a particular need and a basis for it, I don't see how we can break the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this statement was not taken by this Tribunal; it's by the MUP sometime earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I thought this was a general rule by statements, but, you know -- I certainly don't object in principle because I like getting statements in on occasion. But I'm merely quoting the Prosecution since they seem to be having these inflexible rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, do you have any special reasons to tender this document into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It may just be useful for putting in context what Mr. Celanovic has testified to, but apart from that we don't have any special reasons for moving that in, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you have asked some questions based on this document and all the relevant parts is already in the transcript. So this document is not admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. And we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to tank this Trial Chamber, this Tribunal, for having made it possible for me to finally say the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think after the hearing is adjourned, Madam Usher will show you out of the room. And we'll resume at quarter to 11.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before hearing the next witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to raise? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As I think the Court helped us point out, we made a typographical error in the amended indictment motion, which was rather significant. And we also had a hard time with the paragraph numbering, which Ms. Stewart is sorting out. I unfortunately just looked down and see that I don't have the indictment in front of me, so I believe there was a paragraph that needed to be changed -- the letter needed to be changed from -- but I better wait until next time, I apologise, to make the actual change on the record, because I notice I didn't bring it with me. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I hope you could submit your written correction in this respect, because we believe that this mistake, of course, is a typing mistake, but it has great significance to the Defence case. And at the same time, Mr. Karnavas, would you please indicate somehow when are we going to receive your response to that? You know we are working under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was unaware of that, Your Honour. But -- well, to be honest, I saw it. I looked at it. It's Thursday; we got it on Monday. I was hoping I would take a good look at it over the weekend and have something perhaps early next week. That's the best I can do. I can barely keep my nose above the water. As you see this last witness and the next witness we are about to hear are a little challenging, shall we say, in keeping them to sort of answering in a direct way. So anyway, hopefully by the middle of next week. We certainly don't want to prolong providing a response, it's just that with all the other demands that we have with the witnesses it's been impossible to really focus on this. So the weekend, Friday afternoon, Saturday, I'll be spending and devoting my entire time to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Here I would like to remind the parties that according to Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence under (A), the Prosecutor may amend an indictment (iii) seeing that "after the commencement of the presentation of the evidence with leave of the Trial Chamber hearing the case, after having heard the parties." So it depends on the submission of the parties. We might, I just say we might, at this stage to have a hearing on that request, which I believe should be more concentrated on the legal issues, the rights of the accused, rather than the factual issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is this a two-step process or a one-step process? In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What do you mean by one step or two steps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the one step is: Does the Trial Chamber grant leave, that's step number one. Step number two: To what extent will the Trial Chamber accept the modifications that are being added or amended in the indictment itself. So I think I need to challenge both, if I decide to challenge. That is I don't want to prejudge the Prosecution's motion, but I might, in all likelihood, I would say, first argue that the Court should not grant the Prosecution leave, but in the event it does grant it leave I need to at least state why I think perhaps that amended indictment is flawed in other technical matters and how I might be able to assist the Trial Chamber in perhaps making the indictment, you know, more favourable to the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I still can't figure out what is one step and what is two steps. Let me say it clearly that -- sorry. And first of all we have to receive the response from the parties. We have to know whether you agree with it or you have some reasons against it. Secondly, we might have a hearing to hear the parties to let the parties -- to give the parties the opportunity to assist the Trial Chamber on such legal issues as I said before. And after that, we'll consider whether to grant the request or not. And even after that, to my understanding, this decision is subject to appeal. And we might, we might, grant that certification of appeal. I'm not sure because I haven't seen the reasonings of the parties at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we could have this procedure to go as fast as possible, because we are really under pressure at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the next witness, I have to say that we are somehow behind schedule and we only heard two witnesses this week and we have still three witnesses waiting on the list. And, Mr. Karnavas, would you tell us approximately how long that will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I switched the order a little bit to make sure that we would be able to -- we would have two people waiting over the weekend, if that were the case. This next witness as I said is a little bit of a challenge in focusing him to short, concise answers, but I believe we might be able to finish that gentleman today. The next witness would be a little bit shorter. And then the last witness is a little bit longer. I think if we had -- and I'm not suggesting, though I'm not declining the possibility of having an afternoon session tomorrow, there might be a possibility of finishing all the witnesses. But again, it all depends on this witness here. We might not be able -- if we don't finish him today, then all I can expect is to have one more witness tomorrow. For sure he would be able to finish. So we would finish for this week. And then for the following week, I've looked at the list. They seem to be rather shorter and we would be able to make up the ground so we wouldn't lose any time. I will streamline my direct with this witness, in keeping with the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. But I'm sorry to say that we've looked into the schedule and the arrangement of various activities of the Judges, it seems to me impossible for us to have an extra afternoon hearing this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There might be an opportunity next week, but I'm not sure at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for the next witness, are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: J-o-v-a-n, and the last name, I-v-i-c or C with a diacritical mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You're most welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, first of all, where do you live right now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I live in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. These microphones are rather sensitive, so you don't have to shout. They'll pick up the sound. Now -- and what do you do in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I'm a professor of Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long have you been a Russian professor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I've been doing this since 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: From that year, from 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you do your JNA military service?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did. I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: That was in Slovenia, which was a part of Yugoslavia. And I served in a place called Vrhnika which was quite near Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I joined the JNA in 1976 and I completed my service in September 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in 1995, in July, were you a member of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in which unit you were serving.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I was in a unit which controlled all entries and exits from -- to and from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where was that located, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This unit was located at a checkpoint. The checkpoint was called Zuti Most, the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was there a komandir at that location for that unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was that komandir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I myself was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you tell us how many members consisted -- made up this unit. How many members?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: There were four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how many would be there on any particular shift? What was the number for the shift?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: We actually did not have work organised in shifts, and we were all this one shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we talk a little bit about this unit, could you please tell us how long you had been at that location carrying out those functions within the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I was there approximately from the end of May 1994, and then until about a month or two of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that would have been until, say, August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Approximately. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us who was your commander, your immediate commander, your superior officer, that you would report to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about the -- this unit that you belonged to, was this part of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Formally, yes. But actually, we were a separate group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say: "Formally, yes." So let me ask you: Did you have any contact with or were you under the directions of the commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know who the commander of the Bratunac -- oh, no. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I didn't hear the question properly. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Take your time. Just listen to the entire question. Did you take any orders from the commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, since formally you indicated you were a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not, not from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking -- we're not talking about the commander. I'm talking about of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. I did not receive orders from him -- the commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Am I to understand that you had no report duties then to the military police, the commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not have to report to him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you report to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at this point in time I want to discuss your functions at the Zuti Most. Could you please tell us briefly and concisely what your functions were at the Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: My duty was, as well as that of the group working with me, was checking everything that went into Srebrenica and everything that went out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I believe you used the word "control." Could you please tell us what you mean by that, this control or checking.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It means that when I get approval for something to pass by my checkpoint, then I'm supposed to abide by what the paper I got says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, was that for everything that went in and everything that came out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have authority to look into the convoy and to check the items?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have the authority to prevent a convoy from going through to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did, if that is what the paper said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What if you had documentation that matched what was in the convoy, could you on your own stop that convoy, prevent it from going into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Momir Nikolic, could he prevent that from going in?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, he could not do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the commander of the brigade, could he prevent that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No way, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, hypothetically, what if there was an item inside the convoy that was not included in the documentation, how could you handle that situation? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I would stop the convoy and ask Momir Nikolic for instructions or assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would that be with respect to the entire shipment or just the item that wasn't justified on the manifest?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Only that which had not been mentioned in the documentation would have been discussed, that which was controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what if you couldn't get a hold of Momir Nikolic? What if he was unavailable? What would you do then? Who would you contact?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I would call a person from the corps who was in charge of passage through Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why would you not contact Momir Nikolic's commander, that is the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Because he did not have the authority for the passage of convoys through Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you would contact the corps. How would you contact them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I had a wire connection from the checkpoint to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you just call up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'd call up, I'd phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to lean in and speak to the mike. I think it will pick it up, so you can just relax. That's better. Now, did there ever come a time in your experience while you were there as the komandir of the Zuti Most unit when the commander, the then-commander, of the Bratunac Brigade tried to interfere with the passage or with your work with respect to the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The commander before Mr. Blagojevic - his name was Ognjenovic - tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what happened, the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You mean with Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking -- I'm asking for that concrete example.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, once before the fall of Srebrenica -- because the Dutchmen had restricted shipments of fuel, it happened once that the Dutch in their convoy were transporting a certain quantity of fuel that they had not been entitled to. That is to say, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska had not given them permission for that quantity. In that case, according to regular procedure, we exempted that fuel. At the end of the day, I sent a report to the duty officer of the brigade regarding all of this. And in the evening when I came home, around 10.00, Commander Ognjenovic called me; he had seen that report. And he told me to come to the brigade headquarters. I came. The commander said: "What have you done?" I said that I exempted or seized this fuel, because it was not included in the permit. And then he said: "Why didn't you confiscate the convoy?" Because before that there had been some discussions, but this was only verbal, that vehicles transporting a particular cargo for which they did not have permission should be seized as such. I never received such orders in writing. And therefore I did not act in accordance with this, which was mentioned only verbally, and I never seized or confiscated a vehicle. Then Commander Ognjenovic said: "Go out. As of tomorrow, you will not be at Zuti Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Momir Nikolic. I told him of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what did Momir Nikolic tell you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: He said that he would talk to Ognjenovic about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: And then, because he did not manage to get me back to the checkpoint through Ognjenovic, he said that I should go to Popovic, to the corps. He said that he would send me to the corps, to Popovic, to explain what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where was that, sir? Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It was in Vlasenica, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the result of your conversations with Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The result was that Popovic called Ognjenovic. I was there when he did. And he told him to return me to the checkpoint. And then Ognjenovic said that it was for him to decide, that he was the commander of the brigade and that he would not return me to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Very quickly, I think it was within ten days or so, Ognjenovic was removed, and Momir Nikolic returned me to Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in order for you to check the material that was in the convoy, did you receive any paperwork?
