utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, how did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: A member of the military police would bring it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where was the paperwork from? Where did it originate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The paperwork carried the signature of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It arrived in our brigade to the communications section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then from there it would come to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Then somebody from the military police would take it from the communications section and bring it to Zuti Most. Sometimes I would stop by the communications section and pick it up before I went to work. I would pick up that permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us in your example with the fuel that you -- had been confiscated, that you made that report to the brigade, and that's how Ognjenovic learned about it. Would you please tell us what the reporting system was from you backwards. You told us you got documents from main corps; what would you do after a convoy left, went through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: At the end of every day when all the passages envisaged for that day would be completed, I would send a report to the duty officer of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that way they would know whether the convoy had -- what time it went through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then they had information about everything that had happened at the checkpoint on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you some documents. Perhaps you can help us out here. Documents we received from the Office of the Prosecution. And for your convenience and in order to speed up the process a little bit, you'll see that some areas have been premarked so you can focus your attention on those. Now, the first document, which is identified as D173, could you please just look at this document and see if you recognise what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I do. I do recognise it. This is the kind of document that I received, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me walk you through this. I know you're anxious. Let me walk you through step by step. All right. Where is this document from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It comes from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does it have a date on it, if you can read it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 2nd of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all, what is this document? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It is a permit from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for the passage of convoys through Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how do we know it's for Zuti Most? Where do we see that? Could you direct our attention to any particular numbered paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Any other paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number 4. Paragraph number 5. And paragraph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as an example, if we could stay with paragraph 3, if you could tell us what is contained in this paragraph that would be of interest or of importance to you, being that you were at the control sector at that Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is important because I see that I -- that the International Red Cross team from Bijeljina was allowed to enter Srebrenica on the 5th of April, 1995. And to -- no. Not on the same day. On the 8th of April, 1995, they are allowed to return from Srebrenica. And then reference is made to the content of the convoy. That is to say what was to be transported and also the number of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the items that would be in this -- the contents of the convoy, is that what you would be looking for or looking at to ensure that nothing that wasn't included in this paperwork was not among the contents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this particular document, is there any other -- you see some handwriting, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is there a signature as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the signature of Momir Nikolic. And a recommendation addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, whose handwriting is that and whose signature is it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Momir Nikolic, and it's his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what does that state? What is he -- what has he written on this particular document that has come from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: He wrote the following: "Not a single convoy or team of the International Red Cross or any team of the Doctors Without Borders may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you one question here at this point. What if you could not get a hold of Momir Nikolic to get his permission, could you, for instance, contact the commander of the Bratunac Brigade to get his permission for the convoy to go through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I could not. He was not in charge for such passages; the brigade commander was not in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if you couldn't get Momir Nikolic's permission because he was unavailable, where would you -- from whom would you seek permission to allow the convoy to enter Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said. I would have asked the corps if anything was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me show you another document. This one having been marked for identification as D174 -- actually, there are several pages to this. Again, all of these documents have been presented to us by the Office of the Prosecution and bear an ERN number. I want to look at the first document, the first one. Do you recognise the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It is also permission from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for the passage of a convoy or convoys via the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, over here could you point out just very briefly which sections would be significant for you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The only thing of significance to me is the passages through Zuti Most. And here it is indicated the 27th of May, 1995, a Russian convoy has been authorised passage, a Russian convoy transporting humanitarian relief to Srebrenica composed of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't need to go --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: -- nine trucks, 72 -- carrying 72 tonnes of flour. That is for that convoy. And then for the next one, the next convoy which was to enter Srebrenica, which I believe was on the 28th of May, it is illegible here, also 1995. It was also a Russian convoy with nine trucks carrying 72 tonnes of flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that one says Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Gorazde, but below that is Srebrenica. Where we have the approval for the Swedish construction project, approving the entry of one motor vehicle and 10 tonnes of material for the construction project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can stop you here so we can go through this a little quicker. So we see that there are several references from Karakaj to Srebrenica - correct - on these pages?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Karakaj would be in the direction of Zvornik. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think if we look at the top of the paragraph this would consist of a weekly paragraph from the week of May 27 to June 2nd?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The plan for the entry of humanitarian relief deliveries to Srebrenica for that particular week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next document which is attached to this document, which is again 174, there is some handwriting on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, the ERN number is 01331262.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at it. Do you see it? Do you see that page -- that hand --?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, found and looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Step by step. Again. Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I'm a hundred per cent sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you -- we have a translation that was provided to us by the registrar here, but I would like you to read it very slowly and if we could hear the translation to what you read, as opposed to what we have on the document itself. So slowly could you read your own handwriting aloud, that is, so the translators can hear.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: As already said: "My battalion still has the mission to guard the population of the safe haven referred to and consequently to maintain an observation post on the confrontation line." That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to make sure that I have it right, is it "safeguard" or "guard"? Which of the two is on that -- on your document? If you could just read it one more time, sir. Just read it aloud and read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Its mission is to safeguard the population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note it is the same word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the population of the safe haven referred to, and consequently to maintain an observation post -- to have an observation post on the line of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So there's nothing -- so there's nothing in this document that states that you are to make life difficult for the observers on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think there is some confusion in terms of the translation we have received from the interpreters in here. So other than read out what it says, what his handwriting is, I don't think any more can be said. And we heard from the interpreters that I understand the word "guard" can also mean safeguard. So we don't really know what he means. But -- now putting something else to him, I think that's leading, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you read the translations there, then put your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to lay the foundations first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me read to you what was translated, a portion of which I read before we got an objection from Mr. Prosecutor here. This is what was officially translated and please follow along and to see if it's correct. You may wish to put your glasses on because I'm about to read. "As has been said before, my battalion's mission is still to guard the population in the safe area in question and therefore to make life difficult for the observers on the confrontation line." Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is totally the opposite of what it says here. There is no reference to making anything difficult, just to maintain an observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, since that's your handwriting, do you know what is this in relation to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember in connection with what this was written. Perhaps it can be outside the convoy's context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the reason, for the record, that this is being read at the time is because this document followed the previous document, as was provided to us. So we weren't sure whether this was connected. Now, if you could go to the last page, and if we look at the ERN number on that page which is 01331263. It follows the previous page that we just read out. There we have a note, do we not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what does that note state?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is a note from the Main Staff. "We do not consent to having on Wednesday, the 31st of May, 1995 a satellite telex being delivered to Srebrenica with equipment for the requirements of the UNHCR office."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what does this note tell you, being at the checkpoint, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: That means that that is not permitted so it cannot enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what if you were to find this satellite telex and equipment in that particular shipment, what were you to do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I would have called Momir Nikolic, as a rule, that's what I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next line it states: "The convoy leaders will carry manifests of the load and persons they are transporting." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us what significance does that have in relation to what you were doing at the time, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would take this manifest from the convoy leader. I would collate it with the permit which was given to me. And I would see whether they matched, whether the manifest matched the permit. And of course, I would then proceed with checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to show you another document -- you're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to show you another document which has been marked as D175. I would like to focus -- first of all, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, this is a similar document to what we've just been seeing, a weekly plan. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and this again is from the Main Staff, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we have a date on it, do we not, sir, or the period --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention where it says: "Karakaj-Bratunac, two lorries," and then so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether this convoy would have been checked through to Srebrenica or whether this was to remain in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The destination of this convoy was, in fact, then Bratunac so it could not go on to Srebrenica, seeing that its destination in the first place was Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with this -- controlling this particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Because it did not pass by my checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention on the first line. It says: "We consent to implementing the weekly plan of the Belgrade UNHCR." And then it has the authorisation and then the schedule. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from that can you draw any conclusions with respect to the Main Staff's involvement as to the humanitarian aid that would go into places like Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion can be that all passengers through the -- through Republika Srpska at the time, including two towns which were controlled by Serbs, were approved by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the towns that we see on this document, were they all controlled by Serbs at the time, Bijeljina, Vlasenica, Sokolac, Visegrad, Bratunac, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I can see that all these places were controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go through another document. This has been identified as D176 -- actually, there's two parts. 176.1 and 176.2. But as with the previous documents, we will go step by step. Would you please look at the first document, and just from looking at it are you able to recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is a report from the Zvornik Brigade to the Drina Corps command on the passage of a convoy to Srebrenica composed of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Step by step. Let me lead you, please. First of all, what is the date?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 4th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I can direct your attention to the bottom or to the -- towards the end of this regular combat report from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade to the Drina Corps, if I could direct your attention to paragraph number 10. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would you please tell us what does that tell us? What does that convey to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It tells me that all reports on the passage of convoys or namely that all checkpoints sent reports on the passage of convoys to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But on that particular day, 4 July 1995, what conclusions can you draw from paragraph number 10?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: That there are no restrictions on humanitarian assistance being sent to the people of Srebrenica prior to the attack on Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to go step by step. On this particular day, July 4th, it says here: "UNHCR convoy going from Belgrade to Srebrenica, composed of two off-road vehicles, eight trucks, and 12 persons crossed the border at 1000 hours." Okay. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, first of all where would the border be? Which border are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The border would be in Karakaj, in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and this is coming from where? This UNHCR convoy is coming from where?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: From Belgrade. The UNHCR from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, once it crosses the border, assuming that it's heading to Srebrenica, in which direction would it be going?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It would be going from Drinjaca to Bratunac to Zuti Most and then to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look at the next document that's attached to this -- to the one that you're reading, which is marked for identification as D176.2. If you could look at that, sir. And again, step by step. Please look at it, and I'll lead you through with my questions. Do you know what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is a daily -- a regular combat report. Yeah, I know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And what day is it? For what day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It is also the 4th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go down to paragraph number 8, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for the record I'll read it and we'll discuss it. "Convoy passage: An UNHCR Russian convoy entered the area, consisting of two jeeps, eight trucks, and 11 people. Cargo: Food. The convoy left the area without cargo." What does that mean, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It means that our brigade also sent reports to the Drina Corps on the passage of convoys, because this is the same convoy which entered Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would this be the same one that was referred to -- would it appear, I should say, to be the same one, July 4, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same convoy going from Belgrade to Srebrenica and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, assuming the events in Srebrenica commenced on 4 July 1995, from this daily combat report it would appear, would it not, that two days prior to that, on 4 July 1995, a humanitarian convoy went through Srebrenica by way of the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And one last question from this: Can a conclusion be also drawn as to whether the Drina Corps is able to track the passage of convoys from checkpoint to checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is so able, because they were receiving reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go through one last document -- set of documents. This is -- this has been marked as D177. And there is -- as in the previous one, there is a 1 and a 2, two separate documents, though they are -- we'll discuss them together. So it's D177.1 and D177.2. First of all, focus your attention, please, to the first document. Look at it so we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've taken a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And first of all, where is this document from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It is again from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: This is also a permit for carrying out deliveries of humanitarian assistance of the UNHCR from the direction of Belgrade, according to the following scheme or plan. For example, on the 23rd of May, 1995, the entry into Srebrenica is approved of a Russian convoy consisting of six trucks carrying 48 tonnes of flour, 9 tonnes of beans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: And on the very next day, on the 24th of May, 1995, Karakaj to Srebrenica, entry into Srebrenica again is approved of six lorries, also this time carrying 48 tonnes of flour, 48 tonnes of beans, 688 tins of tinned beef, 4 tonnes of sugar, detergent and other requirements, necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just walk you through, because in a couple of minutes we can be through with this document. So if I could direct your attention to the number. Is there a particular -- of this document, a reference number. Do you see it where it states: "Main Staff, Army of Republika Srpska," do you see a reference number there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 06/20-202. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then if we were to go down on this page where perhaps I guess the date would be 21 of May, Karakaj, Srebrenica, do you see that. And it talks about --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see two trucks of --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: The Swedish construction project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we then were to go to the last page of these documents which is for identification purposes D177.2. If you look at that, and if I could just walk you through very quickly. This is a daily combat report, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is from the Bratunac Brigade to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the date is 21 May, 1995. The date at the top, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if I can focus your attention to what you were look at which is paragraph 8. Now, it would appear that if we were to look at this particular paragraph, compare the number from the VRS document that we looked, the Main Staff document, D177.1, we would see that the number corresponds, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if we were to pay close attention to this particular paragraph and then compare this -- the items that appear on this paragraph with the items that are listed or noted in the previous document from the Main Staff, they would match, would they not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this is an example of what you were doing when you indicated that when a convoy would go through to the enclave, you would notify the command so that this information could be put into the daily report and sent to the Drina Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at least this way the corps was know that the convoy had made its way through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I see it's about time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 30 minutes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic, I now want to focus your attention to the period of July 6 and onwards. And as a point of reference, it has been established that July 6th was the day when the events commenced concerning Srebrenica and July 11th was the day that Srebrenica fell. The first question is: Prior to July 6th, did you receive any particular instructions or any unusual instructions, instructions out of the ordinary, during that period?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you informed in any way, in light of your position, your special unit under the command of Momir Nikolic and the corps, of what was going on concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did anything unusual happen between the 6th of July and the 11th of July at the Zuti Most where you were located, that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a day or two before the 11th of July I did notice something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know the exact date? Was it one day or two days before the fall of Srebrenica? And if you don't know, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I just remember that before the fall of Srebrenica a tank close to our checkpoint in the evening was firing at Srebrenica. That was the only unusual thing that happened in terms of operations from Zuti Most towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know who was in the tank, which unit? This is a particular detail that I'm sure the Prosecution would like to know, what unit was operating that tank, if you know.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which unit it belonged to, but that evening I saw Borovcanin there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you know Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How did you know he was Borovcanin if you didn't him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Later on I heard that that was Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You didn't know him at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not know him at the time, and that was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Borovcanin at one point in time, I don't know the exact year, but one or two or three years earlier had been associated with the Bratunac Brigade -- I mean, the -- I'm sorry. The Bratunac police department, MUP. Were you aware of that some time -- a few years earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did any -- did Mr. Borovcanin or any of his men come to you or did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contact, but he sat there at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you have a conversation with him, greet him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No. He was with some men who I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you see Nikolic there at that point in time, and we're speaking about Momir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him that evening. Maybe he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to guess. I'm asking you what you recall and what you know. Do you know whether he was there, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the day that Srebrenica fell, July 11th, 1995, do you recall that day? That's a pretty special day, rather unusual. Do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you on duty that day? That is, were you at your post at the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you -- a detail that we haven't covered. Could you please tell us what your shifts were. What sort of shifts did you and your men have at the Zuti Most? Were you on ...

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: We did not have any shifts. We came in the morning and we waited for all the planned passages for that particular day to take place. Once the approved convoys would pass there, we would go home. We slept at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But surely there must have been somebody guarding or somebody at the checkpoint, the Zuti Most checkpoint, 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: At the time when Srebrenica fell and during those days, on the eve of the fall, we were there round the clock. We were there for 24 hours. We slept at the checkpoint, too. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall on that particular day if anything unusual happened at the checkpoint. What do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I recall some troops that I did not know. And I remember a tank at the checkpoint. I remember some men who I did not know either who had trained dogs. They were waiting there to go towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you notice any DutchBat at that time, any of the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: At that time, they could not come to the checkpoint. I didn't notice them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we know that there was a meeting -- in fact, two meetings in Bratunac with the DutchBat and one with a representative of the Muslim community from Potocari. Were you there when they would have come by and through the Zuti Most on the -- that date, that is July 11, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at that point in time, were the -- was Borovcanin over there? Because you mentioned you saw Borovcanin, you saw this tank, and now you've indicated that there were some soldiers with trained dogs, some units that you didn't recognise. Were they there at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Correction. Borovcanin was there the night before Srebrenica was entered. And these units were there on the day when Srebrenica was entered. There were at Zuti Most on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, a point of clarification. You say "when Srebrenica was entered." Did you go into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on that day -- are we speaking the day the buses went towards Srebrenica? Which day are you talking about? The day that folks entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the day when people were entering Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, are you talking about Potocari or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Potocari, Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We've got to be specific. So let me see if I can get this straight now. What day are you referring to when you say people were entering Potocari. What is that day? Who is entering and what is happening on that day, so we can use that as a reference point?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think that was the first day when the army entered Srebrenica from the other side. These troops at Zuti Most were waiting to go into Potocari because the civilian population was in Potocari. They had no need to go to Srebrenica, these men from Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was that the same day that the buses arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that was the first day, as far as I can remember. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. About what time did the, if you recall, did the DutchBat with the representatives of the Muslim community go by the Zuti Most. Do you know about what time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I know it's a difficult exercise so late in the day, but a couple of issues weren't really said by the witness, for instance that buses arrived and also that representatives of the Muslims came. So if -- I understand Mr. Karnavas, please today, but he has to be non-leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As far as, Your Honour, whether there are issues that are unresolved, the Prosecutor, I am sure, will have the opportunity to cross-examine and resolve any unresolved issues he may have in his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, as a matter of fact, I think you should do your best to establish the day so we could have a clear record here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course it depends on how good the memory of the witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to get back to events and then slowly work that way through, otherwise I would have to lead. But I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the beginning. And I want to focus your attention to the day when the buses went towards Potocari. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When I'm referring to Potocari, I want you to think of Potocari, not Srebrenica. All right. Now, do you recall that day when the buses were going to Potocari, they first started going?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I recall that they were going to Potocari, but whether it was the day when Srebrenica was entered or the following day, that is something I cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, we got that out of the way. How many days were buses going to Potocari, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think they were going for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you saw Mr. Borovcanin and that tank, how many days prior to the buses going to Potocari did you see him? So use the buses going there that first day when you saw them, use that as a focus -- focal point and work backwards, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was two days before the buses went to Potocari, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall how many days before the buses started going to Potocari that you saw DutchBat and any representatives from the Muslim community from Potocari going towards Bratunac, passing through your checkpoint? And I'm talking about the first time.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No. The Muslims did not go to Bratunac before entering Srebrenica, but members of the Dutch Battalion came regularly to discuss things with the representatives of our brigade. Regularly they did that before entering Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's skip that part. Let me focus on the two days that you saw the buses arriving. First of all, do you recall from which direction they were coming? Were they coming from Srebrenica or were they coming from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: They were coming from the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall about what time of day was it when the buses began arriving, the first day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you given any specific instructions on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I was not given any instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Momir Nikolic come by to check up and give any -- give you any instructions or suggestions or any information as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: On the day when Srebrenica was entered, he was at Zuti Most like many others. And it was said that we should provide for the unhindered departure of vehicles from Potocari without keeping them, and that this should evolve without any kind of difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was that the day that the buses were arriving, or was that the previous day? Which of the two, if you remember, and these are important details?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it was the day before the buses left, on the very day when Srebrenica was entered. I remember that it was said then. Now, I cannot remember whether the buses departed on that very same day or the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you see any higher-echelon officers while you were at the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: At the time when Srebrenica was entered, I did not see a single officer from the Bratunac Brigade. I only saw the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic or General Krstic or General Zivanovic or Colonel Beara or Lieutenant Colonel Popovic? Did you see any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Now I am refuting what I said. On the day when Srebrenica was entered, I did see General Mladic. As he was leaving Srebrenica, he passed through my checkpoint with his escort in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what did he do? Did he stop? Did he talk to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: That first time he passed there, he didn't stop at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did anyone else pass through the checkpoint on that day after Mladic, General Mladic, had gone through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, except for the soldiers who entered Potocari afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there were no Dutch Battalion officers going to Bratunac the day that Srebrenica fell after you saw Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think that in the evening the representatives of the Dutch Battalion went to Bratunac, together with the representatives of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was that the same meeting that General Mladic went through your checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The same day, the same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And is that the same evening that you saw Borovcanin, or was that on another day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Borovcanin was there the previous evening, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, during the days when the buses were coming and going, the 12th and the 13th of July, did you go into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How far is Potocari from the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: 2 or 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did any members of your unit go into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you said that there were four of you. How many of the four -- of the three?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who ordered them, if anyone, to go there, if you know, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think they went out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't know whether they were ordered or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they give you a report or did they tell you what was happening once they returned?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- well, they didn't give me a report. They talked to me. It was a private conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- but you indicated as we began that you were the komandir of this unit. That would put you responsible for their activities, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was supposed to be, but there was improvisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what does that mean "improvisation"? Anybody can do whatever they want, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No. It means that it's the winds of war that make things get out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you report their absence to Momir Nikolic, since he was your immediate commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why you didn't report that they had left their posts and had gone into Potocari, assuming that they had not been ordered to go there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: There was no reason for me to talk about it. They could have done so whenever they wanted to do it if there were no obligations at Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during those two days, the 12th and the 13th, did you see Colonel Blagojevic go into Potocari because he had to -- assuming he would have gone through the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic after that one time, that is the day that Srebrenica fell, did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the day when the Muslims were evacuated, but I'm not sure. I think it was the first day of the evacuation and the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us what you noticed when General Mladic was there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: One convoy was returned, and I noticed a man who had climbed up on a truck and was talking to some of the Muslims there who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all this one convoy, who was in the convoy or what was in the convoy that had been returned?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: It was the Dutch convoy. It was the convoy of Dutch vehicles, and the Dutch were evacuating persons who was seriously wounded. That's who was in that convoy. However, the convoy was returned from the Muslim-controlled territory. The Muslims did not want to take their own people in, at least that's the explanation that the leader of the convoy gave to me. And then they came back to me with the intention of going back to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I stopped that, because then they no longer had a permit to go in. It was late at night. And I called the brigade, I called Momir Nikolic. There was no one there to help me. I called the duty officer, and I explained the situation to him. He said: "No one can help you with that." And I said: "General Mladic is there; ask him." But it was already 2.00 in the morning, as far as I can remember. And he said, the duty officer said: "Oh, Mladic is asleep now. Nobody would dare wake him up." So that's how the convoy spent the night there. I was waiting for someone to help me the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did help arrive the following day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, the next morning General Mladic came to Potocari. It was perhaps around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, and he stopped at the checkpoint at Zuti Most. Then he saw one of the soldiers who was clinging on to this truck, as it were, and he was talking to these wounded. And I walked up to the general, in the hope that he would tell me something as to what to do with the convoy. And he asked me: "Who is that guy over there?" And I said: "General, sir, there is nothing I can do about him." And the general told me: "Go away, you bear, you. Why don't you protect the innocent people? Take a gun and shoot him." Then he climbed up on to the truck. He talked for a while to the people there. And then he went to Potocari, in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about the people that were in the convoy? What happened to them, the wounded ones? What do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, this convoy leader told me that he had formidable problems, that three people had died that night at the checkpoint. He asked me what he was to do; there was no way I could help him. But very soon after General Mladic left, somebody - I don't remember who exactly - told me that I was supposed to turn the convoy in the other direction and they should head for Muslim territory again. And that's the way it was. The convoy then went in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And after those two days, how long -- when the buses were coming, the buses and the trucks, did you do anything else, did you have any other duties after those two days after the Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, after that we were there formally. There were no obligations to speak of, because the civilian police came to man the checkpoint very shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to focus your attention on Momir Nikolic, your commander. Now, at that point in time, that is, when you were the komandir at the Zuti Most, were there ever occasions when there would be meetings between Momir Nikolic and the DutchBat, commanders of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Such meetings were held very frequently, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what Momir Nikolic's rank was, his actual rank?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a captain. That was his actual rank, but unofficially another rank was being bandied about as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that "unofficially"? Other higher officers were saying that he was higher than a captain or was Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How did Mr. Nikolic represent himself to the DutchBat? What rank did he allow himself to have?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: What he said and the way I was supposed to address him in the presence of the Dutch was that he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's a higher rank than a captain, for those of us who haven't served?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Definitely, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So not only did he represent himself as a major, but you, too, would have to address him as a major, right, in front of the Dutch?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did he ever also purport to represent himself as the commander of the brigade, or at least give that appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey can object if he wishes. There's no need to be whispering objections to his colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, did you hear the objections raised by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I've heard it before. And I -- it's my recollection that I don't have any problems speaking in whispers to Mr. Karnavas [sic]. I'm trying not to irritate anyone in this, but we occasionally do whisper to each other. It's not meant to be anything very mysterious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the discussions between the counsels within a team is allowed in this courtroom, but the condition is that it should not obstruct the proceedings of this case. If there is an objection raised by the other party, I believe you have to bear that in mind. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Would you be please so kind as to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're focusing on Momir Nikolic. Was there ever an occasion where Momir Nikolic gave the impression that perhaps he was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, to the Dutch, that is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. One could say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you give us just an example, one example, as to when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: For example, I remember this one occasion when representatives of the DutchBat were raising an objection to the effect that at some point at the separation line between the Army of the Republika Srpska and the representative of the Dutch Battalion, these Serbs had opened fire. And then I heard Nikolic say: "I doubt that that is so. My soldiers have no orders to open fire," which actually amounts to his being the commander of all these soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One final question: Do you have an opinion as to Momir Nikolic's character for truthfulness and honesty?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I think that his attitude towards obligations, Momir Nikolic's attitude towards obligations at Zuti Most, where the passages were concerned, was in my view a correct attitude. I think that I can say that. It was a correct attitude, after all. Whereas, in some situations I would have some criticism to level at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm speaking about his honesty. What sort of criticism would you have regarding his honesty, his telling the truth, being an honest person?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, say he was correct in discharging his obligations at Zuti Most. But there are a few things which I didn't like that I could tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Such as?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, such as when there was a meeting, Mr. Karremans would be there, for instance, or before him Mr. Vermeulen, the commander of the Dutch Battalion, with their representatives. And I had this feeling. Now, whether it is a question of Momir Nikolic's character or what, but I somehow felt that he was too conceited and perhaps some people took exception to that. So on such occasions he seemed to go out of his way to arrive at least one minute or several minutes after everybody else had come so that everybody was supposed to wait for Momir. That is one thing that I didn't like, for instance. Or this other example which I gave you a while ago, that he would sometimes use up titles which did not belong to him or he would actually make believe that he was the commander of all the soldiers. Otherwise, I never had any problem in regard to passages on his part. He was always correct as regarded that particular obligation. Otherwise, he was a bit too conceited, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. I appreciate your honesty. I believe there may be some questions from Mr. Jokic's attorney. If not, I'm sure the Prosecutor will have some questions. If you could be as honest and forthright with them as you have been with me, I would appreciate it. And the Judges may have some questions as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Ivic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ivic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, they call me Rus [phoen], the Russian, because I'm a teacher of Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you had interactions with DutchBat, did they also call you Jovo, or were you known also as Jovo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, they called me and everybody else also calls me Jovo. Of course my proper name is Jovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you knew the DutchBat members quite well, I understand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they knew you as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was glad of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you also, apart from speaking Russian and perhaps other languages, you also speak German, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I only speak Russian and 5 per cent of English. I don't speak any German at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did you talk to the members of the DutchBat, in what language?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I talked to them in a limited way. I would say something in English, and then I also sought, if I needed to have a lengthy conversation with them on some subject, I sought the services of an interpreter. And an interpreter would be -- would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if you would -- I think you have told us earlier that you had a wire line to the corps. Is that correct? Telephone connection to the corps.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also had such a connection with the Dutch -- or rather, the Dutch checkpoint which was near mine, as well as with the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember which Dutch checkpoint you were connected to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: There was a Dutch checkpoint at the separation line, and we also had a checkpoint at the line of separation. So we had to exchange information. It was dangerous to go from point to point; we had to have a connection, a communication connection, which was in fact established on my insisting. Mr. Boering, I believe, ensured this connection for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it you occasionally would pick up the phone and call this DutchBat post. That's what the purpose was of that phone connection?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just incidentally, when you talked to the corps, who was on the other line of, you know, the phone conversation when you talked to the corps? I believe you said in Vlasenica. Whom did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Probably the duty officer of the brigade would answer the call, and through him I would ask for my party -- or rather, for the person in charge of the convoys in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about the corps, and you responded by saying you would talk probably to the duty officer of the brigade. Did you mean brigade or did you mean or say corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I -- slip of the tongue. I meant of the corps. Yes, slip of the tongue. Sorry. Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's change subjects and go to the convoys. You were shown a few exhibits about weekly plans to allow convoys through to the enclaves, such as Srebrenica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these trucks, these few trucks which passed your checkpoint, do you know what happened to them, where they were discharged? Did you follow the movements later?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about this convoy which came back at the time of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. I'm not talking about convoys with wounded. I'm talking about the convoys with supplies and goods in their --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which came from outside --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- towards the enclaves. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do. Yes. And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether these convoys, the goods actually reached their destination, be it in Potocari or Srebrenica? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, my task was to let them pass through the checking point. And what happened with them -- to them at the -- in the adversary's territory, I don't know. But I suppose that it reached its desired and intended destination after having passed through the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you don't know whether the population, for instance, of Srebrenica actually received those goods?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: How could I have known? I don't know. That is enemy territory. How could I have found out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many people were in the enclave of Srebrenica whose entries, as you told us this morning, you sort of guarded, checked? Do you know how many people were living inside the enclave in need of food and supplies? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was different information as to the number of people who lived there, different figures were being given ranging up to even 50.000. But I don't know what their exact number was; this is the figure that I heard from some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know that these people were -- whatever the figure is we heard, 40.000, 50.000, do you know that these people were dependent on those goods and supplies that entered Srebrenica? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I know, of course, that they needed this, that they had formidable problems because of the shortage of food. In fact, some people even got in touch with the Muslims at the line of separation, and they told them all sorts of stories, how they had no salt, how they had virtually nothing, how they were practically starving. And this was common knowledge that they lacked many a thing, at least that is the kind of information that reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also knew that DutchBat was inside there, in desperate need also of their supplies?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Dutch only had problems with fuel in the last days. Because they had all sorts of goods, or rather, all sorts of foodstuffs there which they left behind after they left, meaning they had no problems with food but just with fuel. Tonnes of food were driven away from their base after they had departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, you weren't aware of that in those days, between 11th -- between 8th and 11th of July, the observers inside the enclave described the food situation as: Hopeless. That it was a food stocking UNHCR warehouse was almost zero. You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you were in charge of that checkpoint at Zuti Most, and you didn't allow food and other supplies into the enclave, thus furthering the crises the people were suffering already. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are not familiar with things. You cannot put it this way. It was not I who forbid anything. I was given permission whether to let a convoy pass through or not. I was neutral myself. I was only too glad to help, but nothing depended on me. I described the procedure which was to be followed regarding the permission for entry and exit a while ago. I was only a technical person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So despite the fact that you knew the situation was critical, you still maintained this extremely strict policy of not allowing food sufficient into the enclave; you just followed the orders you were given. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just followed the orders that I was given, and I didn't give it much thought. I didn't like it. It hurt me to see people starving, but my task was to execute orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were part of the concept we just described in this courtroom as convoy -- as terror convoy. You were a part of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is really getting out of control. He's indicated the process. He gets orders from the Main Staff. Now, if Mr. Waespi wants to lay a foundation as to how this gentleman was involved in some kind of terror -- convoy terror or whatever term he's using, fine. But I think this is out of line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's a little bit out of the limits. If you want to pursue this question, you have to explain to this witness what is the terror convoy, or you may simply rephrase your question, but your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, Witness, were there other ways for convoys to go into the enclave than the one you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to reply to this question and to say this at the same time, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: There was no other way for a convoy to enter Srebrenica except through Zuti Most. And the other thing which I wanted to say is this: There is a book which the Muslims of Srebrenica - let me say this to you - which the Muslims of Srebrenica wrote which also mentions a Professor Jovo. And people who spent the entire war in Srebrenica say at Zuti Most: There was Jovo, the Russian, the type of the good teacher guy. The Dutch also published a book which I have also read. And in that book they say: At Zuti Most, the checkpoint was manned by Jovo. And they also say -- this doctor whose name I cannot recall, he's from Amsterdam, a Dutchman, who is in charge of this department for Srebrenica events in the Dutch institute. He talked to me in Bratunac. Mind you, this is what he told me, via his interpreter: We have heard a thousand of nice stories about you and your checkpoint from our soldiers, and we want to talk to you. So please bear with me. How can you ask me this demonising question, legally speaking? And words do have a very deep meaning for me. I studied language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on then to the convoy you have mentioned I believe -- or which was mentioned, an UNHCR convoy which may have reached the enclave on the 12th or perhaps on the 13th of July. Do you remember an UNHCR convoy coming alongside your checkpoint which was manned by a Russian and perhaps a Korean woman? Do you remember a convoy consisting of a few white vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Did you say on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A convoy from UNHCR or organised by UNHCR consisting of five white trucks. There was a Russian person leading the convoy and perhaps a young Korean woman. Do you remember that convoy on the 12th or the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that. It was chaos. I cannot remember the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Maybe if you told me something else, perhaps that could jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, were there more UNHCR convoys in those critical days after the fall of Srebrenica, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th? Were there more UNHCR convoys?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I don't think so. There is no reason for convoys to go there because the population had left. Where would they go? Who would they go to when there were no inhabitants left? There was no reason for humanitarian convoys after the fall of Srebrenica. There was no logic. The population had left, so who would anything be taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that's fine. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I don't think there were any convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to the 11th of July, the night of the 11th of July, and I believe you saw Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Was it the 10th or the 11th? I can't remember. But one evening just before the fall of Srebrenica, I did see him at my checkpoint. I don't know exactly which evening it was, but it was just before the fall of Srebrenica. Whether it was one or two evenings before that, I can't remember. Perhaps even three, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And there were quite a few people with him, a few soldiers around him.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could not say quite a few, but there was a group of people there with him and I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they stayed the night over there in a ditch awaiting further action?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. No. It's not a trench or any such thing. It's a -- there's this container and then there's this asphalt road. I don't know whether it was his soldiers or not. He was there, but somebody was firing from the tank. Now, I don't know whether it was his soldiers firing from the tank, but he was there. And they didn't spend the night there. It was impossible to spend the night where I was. There were no conditions for that kind of thing there. There was only just this one trench and there were no trenches there. There was just this one container, and then they returned somewhere to Bratunac or wherever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to interrupt. Witness, I understand you are eager to give your evidence, but your voice is loud enough. You don't have to approach the microphone. I believe after this sitting the interpreters could not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat this, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I mean that you don't have to approach the microphone. Your voice is loud enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a professional deformity. It comes with my line of work, teaching in a school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that, yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic, the next morning or the following morning after these people, Mr. Borovcanin, stayed there, there was an advance, I believe you have told us, towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: So Borovcanin did not spend that night there. He was there for a while. The following day, there were some soldiers there at the checkpoint with a tank. There were a lot of them. I think it was that day - I am sure, actually - when they entered Srebrenica. Whereas, these people were coming through Zuti Most going to Potocari. That's when that unit with the trained dogs was there, too. They all went to Potocari. Quite simply, that's where the Dutch raised the barrier and they went through their checkpoint as well. So there were no incidents involving the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that. Right now, did you have a minefield, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. It was not my task to know about things like that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying you don't know whether there was a minefield in your area? Wasn't that dangerous?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a minefield. That was not my task to establish a minefield, or do I don't know what. If there was a minefield somewhere, it was apart from the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a document which has been marked as P159. And I would like to draw everybody's attention on page 2, the second paragraph under the heading of 12th July. And in your -- Mr. Ivic in your B/C/S version it is also on page 2, the top paragraph. And let me just read out what it says here. "Between" -- and it concerns, as I said, 12th of July, 1995. "Between 0500 and 0630 hours, the pioneers of the Bratunac Brigade, led by Captain Gavric, cleared a passage through a minefield or groups of mines towards Budak or immediately around the Zuti Most/Potocari road. Members of the 1st Company of the Zvornik Special Police Unit, led by a pioneer from the Bratunac Brigade, set off through the cleared passages towards Potocari to create the conditions for the introduction of hardware." And then it talks about the casualty of a person. Somebody was killed, died, in this course. And let me finish with the last sentence. "The first task - to take control of the UN checkpoint on Zuti Most - was completed successfully without incidents. The Dutch UN members did not react." Now, does that refresh your memory about how things occurred that morning? Do you remember anything of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to give me some more information. Now I remember this; now I do remember it. But this minefield is 800 metres away from my checkpoint, to the right. And from Zuti Most towards Potocari, even if there had been a minefield, I could not have reacted. Those were somebody's orders that had nothing to do with me. Other people were entrusted with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying you had nothing to do with anything that is written in here, not the minefield and not --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing whatsoever. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about the "take control of the UN checkpoint on Zuti Most," were you involved in that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The soldiers went up there, and I stayed at my checkpoint. I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, that's not what happened. Didn't you pick up your phone in the morning between 8.00 and 10.00 and call the Dutch checkpoint? Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that on several occasions, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm talking about that morning. Did you pick up the phone that morning and talk to the members of DutchBat, of this checkpoint that had to be abandoned afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I told them that this duty officer had called me - or I can't remember - from the Bratunac Brigade, that now this tank which was at my checkpoint would go to Potocari, along with a lot of troops. I was told to call the checkpoint to say that nothing bad would happen to people at the Dutch checkpoint. These troops were not interested in the Dutch. "Do not put up any resistance." That is what I was told to say. "Do not shoot. Our soldiers are not going to touch you; they're not going to fire a single bullet. The aim of the army is to reach Potocari." I followed that. I remembered and I am telling you quite literally what happened. A soldier from the Dutch checkpoint raised the barrier for our tank to pass by, and nothing else happened, nothing bad happened. That's what I mean. They continued their journey, and there is no way I can know what happened after that. That is how I prevented an incident from breaking out there, but it's not that I wanted to do I don't know what to jeopardise the Dutch in any way. I just conveyed a message from the brigade so that there would be no incident there, and nothing did happen. And I am pleased that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that is a convenient time to break, because I am about to go into another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please tell me how much time do you still need to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it would be probably another half an hour, perhaps even a little bit more. But certainly no more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, Witness, I'm afraid that we have to keep you here in The Hague for another day because we did not finish your testimony. And during your stay here, you have to remember that you have under oath, so please do not talk to anybody about your testimony and please do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: at 1.44 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
